summary:
Consensual same-sex sexual acts between adults in private were not enforced after a 1953 attorney-general directive and a 1963 Supreme Court ruling, and the Knesset formally removed them from the criminal code in 1988; the age of consent is 16 for both heterosexual and homosexual acts. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation has been prohibited in employment since 1992, with exemptions for religious organisations, extended in 1997 to defamation motivated by sexual orientation under the Libel and Slander Law, and in 2000 to products, services and entry into places of entertainment and public places. Every violent crime motivated by sexual orientation is treated as a hate crime carrying double punishment.

Legal recognition of sex reassignment dates to 1986. Since 2015 the Health Ministry has allowed transgender people to change legal gender without undergoing surgery, and in 2024 the Knesset passed a law permitting removal of a previous name from identity cards, where Israeli law had required individuals to record all previous names regardless of gender identity. A June 2013 Knesset bill to eliminate gender markers on national identity cards did not pass, so markers continue to appear on the cards.

Border and airport screening can turn on surgical status. A first-person account published in Haaretz on 3 May 2023 documented a transgender traveller subjected to gender-identity humiliation at an Israeli airport, with security personnel insisting that without surgery the traveller remained male. In 2023 Israel Police adopted a new regulation governing the searching of transgender people, a protocol change following complaints about humiliating searches of trans detainees and travellers.

Official data reported in 2025 shows homophobic and transphobic violence in Israel rose during that year, and Ynet reported anti-LGBTQ violence at a record high, describing dating-app traps and organised ambushes used to lure victims into attacks. These figures are published as anti-LGBTQ totals rather than trans-specific counts, and no population denominator accompanies them, so they establish direction of travel and documented method rather than a comparative rate.

Public assembly has been repeatedly targeted. Jerusalem Pride was initially banned by municipal order until a court overturned the ban; at the 2005 march Yishai Schlissel stabbed three people and received a 10-year sentence, and after his 2015 release he stabbed six marchers, killing teenage girl Shira Banki. On 1 August 2009 an armed attacker killed two people and injured 15 at a lesbian and gay centre in Tel Aviv. The 2025 Tel Aviv Pride, dated 13 June, was cancelled by the municipality after Israeli strikes on Iranian targets, while in 2026 the Jerusalem Municipality raised the Pride flag for the first time along the route from Sacher Park to the Knesset. Israel's first LGBT pride march was held on 17 September 1977 and Tel Aviv's first Pride parade in 1993.

Gender-affirming care is routed through the Committee for Sex Reassignment at Sheba Medical Center in Tel HaShomer, composed of an endocrinologist, a urologist and a plastic surgeon and organised by the Health Ministry, and all sex reassignment surgery in Israel is performed by Dr. Haim Kaplan at Sheba under the committee's approval. Approval is difficult to obtain because of stringent opinions on gender dysphoria. Historically the state blocked such care: Attorney General Haim Cohn blocked Rina Natan's sex reassignment surgery in 1954. In July 2025 the High Court blocked a fast-track attempt to undo a gender change, holding that the 2021 certificate "remains valid."

Conversion therapy is restricted but not prohibited. On 14 February 2022 Health Minister Nitzan Horowitz issued an executive directive banning licensed medical professionals, including psychologists, social workers and Ministry of Health-licensed therapists, from conducting it; the directive does not bind rabbis, clergy or alternative practitioners and has not been codified into law by the Knesset. A February 2016 Knesset bill to ban it for minors failed 37-45, the Israel Medical Association banned members from performing it in January 2019, and in July 2020 MPs passed a bill to begin outlawing it that required two further approvals. The governing coalition defeated a bill to ban conversion therapy on 24 February 2016.

Detention carries an isolation-based default. A law-journal article documents that Israel's response to transgender prisoners' vulnerability has been to isolate or segregate them rather than place them in facilities matching their gender identity. In an October 2019 precedent-setting case an Israeli court ordered the Israel Prison Service to provide hormone replacement therapy to a trans woman prisoner and transfer her from a male prison to a female one after a civil-liberties petition; she was initially held in a separate wing of the women's prison, and a further petition was prepared to have her housed with the general population. Trans women have at times been held in men's prisons in Israel, and placement has been decided case by case by the courts.

Same-sex marriage cannot legally be performed in Israel because there is no civil non-religious marriage, but since 2006 Israeli law recognises civil same-sex marriages performed elsewhere for registration with the same legal rights, and Israel was the first country in Asia to recognise unregistered cohabitation between same-sex couples. In December 2016 Attorney General Avichai Mandelblit instructed the Interior Ministry to give same-sex couples the same citizenship rights as opposite-sex couples, after same-sex spouses of Israeli citizens had previously waited up to seven years for citizenship and typically received only permanent residency. In December 2004 the Tel Aviv District Court ruled the government acted illegally in trying to deport the Colombian partner of a gay Israeli soldier, extending a 1999 Supreme Court rule barring deportation of foreign nationals married to Israeli citizens to common-law and same-sex couples, and in March 2008 the Interior Ministry granted a residency permit to a gay Palestinian from Jenin citing danger to his life in the West Bank.

Public attitudes and legislative behaviour diverge on relationship recognition. A Channel 10 survey reported by the Times of Israel found majority public support for same-sex marriage while half of lawmakers declined to state a position, including a culture minister who has marched in the Pride parade.
tangentialFactors:
Haaretz reported on 24 February 2025 that inflammatory messaging from the United States was affecting Israel's transgender community, with trans Israelis describing heightened fear as US discourse spilled into the local climate. The reported effect is one of atmosphere and personal security rather than a change in Israeli law.

Reproductive and family formation rules have moved through the courts. A July 2018 surrogacy law excluded single men and same-sex couples; the High Court of Justice ruled on 27 February 2020 and the Supreme Court unanimously on 11 July 2021 that the ban violated equality and the right to parenthood, effective 12 January 2022. Between 2008 and 2017 only 3 of 550 same-sex couples seeking to adopt succeeded, against more than a thousand heterosexual couples, until the government reversed course in August 2017 under Supreme Court pressure, and the Knesset voted in July 2018 to keep single men and same-sex couples out of surrogacy.

Access rules outside gender care also differ by orientation. Since 1 June 2017 gay and bisexual men could donate blood following a one-year deferral, a January 2018 Health Ministry pilot allowed donation regardless of last sex, and from October 2021 donation has been allowed regardless of when donors last had sex. In April 2020 the Beersheba Magistrate's Court ordered a local print shop to compensate an LGBTQ rights group after it refused to print posters, holding that where beliefs conflict with the necessity of serving all comers in public space, the latter value prevails.

Scale of assembly is frequently cited as a counterpoint to the violence record: the 2018 Aguda-organised LGBTQ strike drew over 100,000 people to a Tel Aviv rally, and an estimated 250,000 marched in Tel Aviv Pride in June 2022. Community infrastructure includes the Municipal LGBT Community Center opened in Tel Aviv in 2008, described as the first of its kind in the country, and the Jerusalem Open House, which staged the 21 June 2007 Jerusalem parade after police allocated thousands of personnel to secure the area; a central Jerusalem square is to be renamed "Tolerance Square" in memory of Shira Banki, and in 2026 the Jerusalem Municipality hung Pride flags with the Hebrew inscription "equality in life" along the parade route.

The criminalisation regime has a mandated-era lineage: under the British Mandate, official questionnaires documented "unnatural" sexual expression including sodomy between school boys, and Britain pushed criminalisation into Palestinian schools and society, a policy carried into the Israeli state. In 1943 the Acre district court tried Mustafa Naif, aged 16, alongside Mustafa Zaharan for sodomy; Naif recanted to protect his friend, was convicted of perjury instead, and faced a sodomy charge carrying up to 10 years' imprisonment. That charge no longer exists following the 1988 repeal.
localsOnly:
The Israel Defense Forces does not consider gender dysphoria a disqualifying condition and treats transition-specific medical treatment, hormone replacement therapy, sex reassignment surgery and counseling as medically necessary for those diagnosed with transsexualism, paying for those treatments. Gender-specific army regulations, including length of service, which gender to be housed with, and whether to wear a male or female uniform, are determined case by case for transgender soldiers. Because law makes it difficult to begin transition until age 18 and does not normally allow surgery before age 21, only Shachar Erez has undergone surgery while serving, as the first openly transgender officer. Many draftees diagnosed with gender dysphoria can receive an exemption from military service at their own request, and IDF policy does not prohibit intersex persons from service. Openly gay, lesbian and bisexual soldiers have served without hindrance in all branches since the IDF opened the draft to all regardless of sexual orientation in 1993 and ceased linking orientation to security clearances in 1998.

Payment for gender-affirming care runs through the public health insurance system only on approval by the Committee for Sex Reassignment, and because approval is hard to obtain many transgender Israelis pay out of pocket for hormone replacement therapy or travel abroad for surgery.

Israel Prison Service practice on transgender detainees is governed by the 2019 court order and subsequent case-by-case review, with segregation from the general population remaining the documented default management approach in the absence of a court order.

Community and organisational space exists but registration is contested: Outright International's country page, last updated 12 March 2026, states that LGBTI organisations cannot register in Israel. The 1 August 2009 attack killed two people and injured 15 at a lesbian and gay centre in Tel Aviv, and the Jerusalem Open House operates in the capital.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source at legalclarity.org, a page addressing trans rights in Israel covering laws, protections and gaps, returned HTTP 404 at research time and contributed nothing to this assessment; its content is unverified here.

Outright International's country page, last updated 12 March 2026, states that there is no legal gender recognition in Israel. This is unresolved against the 2015 Health Ministry policy permitting legal gender change without surgery and the 2024 Knesset law on removing previous names from identity cards, which are documented elsewhere in this dossier. The nature of the discrepancy, whether Outright is applying a narrower standard of recognition, is not sourced.

The same Outright page states that LGBTI organisations cannot register in Israel. No corroborating source in this inventory supports or contradicts that claim, and it remains unresolved.

Violence statistics cited for 2025 are published as anti-LGBTQ aggregates without trans-specific breakdown, without incident counts in the material reviewed, and without a population denominator. Ynet's characterisation of anti-LGBTQ violence as a record high carries no stated period or denominator in the material reviewed. None of these figures supports a per-capita comparison with Israel's general homicide rate, and no such comparison is made here.

Whether the conversion therapy directive of 14 February 2022 has since been codified into statute by the Knesset is not established in the sources reviewed; the most recent legislative event documented here is the July 2020 bill passing a stage that required two further approvals.
